## Introduction

The Iris dataset, obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, contains measurements from 150 iris flowers belonging to three species: setosa, versicolor, and virginica. Each species is represented by 50 observations. For each flower, four measurements were recorded in centimetres: sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width. These measurements give us a way to analyze whether these physical characteristics can distinguish between different iris species.

The research question for this analysis is: Can we predict an iris flower's species from its sepal and petal measurements?

To answer this question, we use supervised machine learning to classify flowers into one of the three species based on their measurements. We compare a baseline dummy classifier, k-nearest neighbours, and logistic regression using cross-validation. The best performing model is then evaluated on a held-out test set to assess how accurately it predicts the species of previously unseen flower data.

This analysis shows how relatively simple classification methods can identify patterns in biological measurements. It also helps us understand which species are easier to distinguish and where classification errors may occur.

## Methods

The Iris dataset was obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and contains 150 flowers from three species: setosa, versicolor, and virginica. Each flower has four measurements in centimetres: sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width. The goal is to predict the species using these measurements.

The dataset was downloaded and saved locally. During cleaning, empty rows were removed and species names were simplified. The cleaned data was then divided into training (70%) and test (30%) sets using stratified sampling to keep the proportion of each species. A random seed of 522 was used for reproducibility.

Exploratory data analysis was performed only on the training data to avoid data leakage. We calculated the mean and standard deviation of each measurement by species, examined their distributions using histograms, and created a scatter plot comparing petal length and width.

Three classification models were compared: a dummy classifier, k-nearest neighbours (kNN), and logistic regression. The dummy classifier provided a baseline, while kNN classified flowers using their five nearest neighbours. The measurements were standardized for kNN and logistic regression using pipelines to prevent data leakage during cross-validation.

We compared the models using five-fold cross-validation, evaluating their mean accuracy and variation across folds. Accuracy was chosen because the species are equally represented in the dataset. Logistic regression was selected because it achieved similar accuracy to kNN with less variation. Finally, the selected model was evaluated on the held-out test set using accuracy and a confusion matrix.

### Data download

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/iris/iris.data"
raw_path = "../data/raw/iris.data"

iris_raw = pd.read_csv(url, header=None)
iris_raw.to_csv(raw_path, header=False, index=False)
```

### Data cleaning

```{python}
import pandas as pd

column_names = ["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width", "species"]

iris = pd.read_csv(raw_path, header=None, names=column_names)
iris = iris.dropna(how="all")
iris["species"] = iris["species"].str.replace("Iris-", "", regex=False)

iris.to_csv("../data/processed/iris_clean.csv", index=False)

iris.shape
```

### Train/test split

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train_df, test_df = train_test_split(
    iris, test_size=0.3, stratify=iris["species"], random_state=522
)

train_df.to_csv("../data/processed/iris_train.csv", index=False)
test_df.to_csv("../data/processed/iris_test.csv", index=False)

train_df["species"].value_counts()
```

### Exploratory data analysis (training data only)

```{python}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and standard deviation (cm) of each measurement by species in the training data."

summary_table = (
    train_df.groupby("species")
    .agg(["mean", "std"])
    .round(2)
)
summary_table
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of each flower measurement by species in the training data."

import altair as alt

train_long = train_df.melt(id_vars="species", var_name="measurement", value_name="cm")

alt.Chart(train_long).mark_bar(opacity=0.6).encode(
    x=alt.X("cm:Q", bin=alt.Bin(maxbins=20), title="Measurement (cm)"),
    y=alt.Y("count():Q", stack=None, title="Number of flowers"),
    color=alt.Color("species:N", title="Species"),
).properties(
    width=220, height=150
).facet(
    facet=alt.Facet("measurement:N", title=None), columns=2
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-petals
#| fig-cap: "Petal length versus petal width by species in the training data."

alt.Chart(train_df).mark_circle(size=60, opacity=0.6).encode(
    x=alt.X("petal_length:Q", title="Petal length (cm)"),
    y=alt.Y("petal_width:Q", title="Petal width (cm)"),

```

### Model comparison with cross-validation

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cv
#| tbl-cap: "5-fold cross-validation accuracy on the training data."

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X_train = train_df.drop(columns="species")
y_train = train_df["species"]
X_test = test_df.drop(columns="species")
y_test = test_df["species"]

models = {
    "Dummy (most frequent)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "k-nearest neighbours": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()),
    "Logistic regression": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
}

cv_rows = []
for name, model in models.items():
    scores = cross_validate(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5, return_train_score=True)
    cv_rows.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Mean train accuracy": round(scores["train_score"].mean(), 3),
        "Mean validation accuracy": round(scores["test_score"].mean(), 3),
        "SD validation accuracy": round(scores["test_score"].std(), 3),
    })

cv_results = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows)
cv_results
```

## Results

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

final_model = models["Logistic regression"].fit(X_train, y_train)
test_predictions = final_model.predict(X_test)
test_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, test_predictions)
round(test_accuracy, 3)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-confusion
#| tbl-cap: "Confusion matrix of the logistic regression model on the test set."

pd.crosstab(
    y_test, test_predictions, rownames=["Actual species"], colnames=["Predicted species"]
)
```

The exploratory data analysis revealed differences in flower measurements across the three iris species. As shown in @tbl-summary, setosa had the smallest average petal length (1.44 cm) and width (0.23 cm), followed by versicolor (4.24 cm and 1.33 cm) and virginica (5.49 cm and 2.04 cm). The distributions in @fig-distributions showed that petal measurements separated the species more clearly than sepal measurements, which had lots of overlap. Similarly, the scatter plot in @fig-petals showed that setosa formed a distinct cluster, while versicolor and virginica had more overlap. These findings suggest that petal measurements are particularly useful for distinguishing iris species.

As shown in @tbl-cv, both k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression achieved a mean cross-validation accuracy of 94.3%, substantially outperforming the dummy classifier's accuracy of 33.3%. Logistic regression had a slightly lower standard deviation across validation folds (0.047 compared with 0.056), indicating more consistent performance.

The final logistic regression model achieved 97.8% accuracy on the held-out test set, correctly classifying 44 out of 45 flowers. The confusion matrix in @tbl-confusion shows that all 15 setosa and 15 versicolor flowers were classified correctly, while one of the 15 virginica flowers was incorrectly classified as versicolor.

Overall, these results indicate that the four flower measurements can predict iris species with very high accuracy, although a little confusion remains between virginica and versicolor.

## Discussion

The results support our research question by showing that iris species can be predicted accurately using sepal and petal measurements. As expected, differences in flower measurements allowed the models to distinguish between species. Both k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression achieved 94.3% mean cross-validation accuracy, outperforming the dummy classifier's 33.3%. Logistic regression was selected because it had slightly less variation across validation folds.

The final model achieved 97.8% test accuracy, correctly classifying 44 out of 45 flowers. The only error was a virginica flower classified as versicolor, consistent with the overlap between these species observed during exploratory analysis. All setosa flowers were classified correctly.

One limitation is the small dataset of 150 flowers, with only 45 used for testing. The analysis also assumes that the dataset is representative of future flowers, which may not be true. The equal representation of species and use of only four measurements may potentially make the model less reliable on other datasets.

Overall, the findings demonstrate that simple machine learning models can effectively classify iris species. Future work could explore hyperparameter tuning and testing on larger datasets to determine whether this performance holds for more diverse flowers.
